title: Direct vs hybrid, for 7 algorithm families
shows: Each algorithm trained (a) directly on log(rate) with all features including a time-trend feature, (b) on the residual of the Ridge base. Same folds, same rows, same metric. Bars clipped at 6% (k-NN and MLP direct are far worse).
finding: The hybrid wins for every family, by 0.5–1.0 points for tree models. Reason: trees cannot extrapolate. Given a trend feature, a tree predicts the same value for every date after its last split, so direct tree models under-predict later months (negative bias in folds 1 and 3, next chart). The Ridge base carries the trend forward; the tree only learns patterns that repeat (geography, interactions). k-NN and MLP direct fail badly: unscaled time extrapolation and no built-in log-linear structure.
decision: Use the hybrid structure for the final model.

title: Why direct trees lose: bias
shows: Mean signed % error per fold (+ = over-prediction) for three tree learners, direct (dashed) vs hybrid (solid).
finding: Direct tree models (all five) are 1.1–2.9% too low in folds 1 and 3: they freeze the price level at the end of training. Hybrids stay within ±0.7% there. In fold 2 every model over-predicts by ~1.5% because the trend estimated from Jan–Jun alone was too steep (see checks).

title: Leaderboard of all 21 candidates
shows: Mean clean-label MAPE over the 3 time folds (bars) and each fold separately (markers). Teal = chosen ensemble, gold = other ensembles. The stacked ensemble has scores for folds 2–3 only (its weights need an earlier fold), so its bar is not directly comparable. Not shown (MAPE > 6%): Neural net (MLP) — direct, k-Nearest Neighbours — direct.
finding: Three tiers: (1) hybrids and their ensembles at 1.6–1.9%; (2) direct tree models at 2.2–2.7%; (3) linear/GLM at 2.8% and the $/mile baseline at 4.6%. Ridge and the Gamma GLM are indistinguishable, so the log-normal Ridge is not losing anything versus a GLM made for positive skewed targets.

title: Is the ensemble's gain real?
shows: Difference in MAPE between each candidate and the original Ridge + LightGBM, with 95% confidence intervals from a bootstrap over dates (2,000 resamples; whole days are resampled because loads on the same day share market conditions).
finding: LightGBM + XGBoost + Extra Trees: -0.072 points over all folds (CI -0.090 to -0.055, better on 73% of dates) and -0.010 on fold 3 (CI -0.024 to +0.004: no loss). Single learners are within ±0.02 points of LightGBM (XGBoost, HistGradientBoosting) or clearly worse on the most recent fold (Random Forest / Extra Trees alone lose 0.13–0.15 points). Combining tree types that make different errors (boosting vs randomised bagging) is what helps.
decision: Chosen model: Ridge base + equal-weight average of LightGBM, XGBoost and Extra Trees residual models. Rule applied: best mean across folds, provided it is not significantly worse on the most recent fold. Gain is modest ($2.0 MAE) at the cost of ~3× training time.

title: Simple averaging vs learned stacking
shows: Left: non-negative stacking weights learned walk-forward (only earlier folds' predictions). Right: fold MAPE of each ensemble (stacking has no fold-1 score because no earlier fold exists).
finding: Learned weights jump around between folds (e.g. MLP gets 38% from fold 1, 0% from folds 1–2) and the stacked ensemble is the worst ensemble. With only 2–3 folds the weights over-fit the specific market of the earlier months.
decision: Use fixed equal weights: nothing to over-fit.

title: Accuracy vs training cost
shows: Mean MAPE against fit time on a 2-core machine. (h) = hybrid, (d) = direct.
finding: The chosen ensemble trains in ~7 s per fold; still trivial for daily retraining.
